# CRW-941 (sed script writes, sort -o, script files, in-place) read the way getopt_long reads GNU options: any unambiguous
# prefix of a long option names it (re-check of 2026-10-09 on dev 09e5c5bcc: sort --o, --ou and the rest of the prefixes of
# --output were not read; the verifier added sed --expression with a separate script word).

=== CRW-941-S01 | W
--why --o=FILE is an unambiguous GNU prefix of --output (getopt_long): the file is written.
sort --o={MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S02 | W
--why --o FILE (separate value), the shortest prefix of --output.
sort --o {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S03 | W
--why --ou=FILE, prefix of --output.
sort --ou={MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S04 | W
--why --ou FILE, prefix of --output.
sort --ou {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S05 | W
--why --out=FILE, prefix of --output.
sort --out={MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S06 | W
--why --out FILE, prefix of --output.
sort --out {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S07 | W
--why --outp=FILE, prefix of --output.
sort --outp={MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S08 | W
--why --outp FILE, prefix of --output.
sort --outp {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S09 | W
--why --outpu=FILE, prefix of --output.
sort --outpu={MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S10 | W
--why --outpu FILE, prefix of --output.
sort --outpu {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S11 | W
--why --output FILE, the full name with a separate value.
sort --output {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S12 | W
--why -oFILE, the attached short form.
sort -o{MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S13 | W
--why -o FILE, the separate short form.
sort -o {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S14 | W
--why -ro FILE, a bundle that ends in o takes the next word.
sort -ro {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S15 | W
--why -roFILE, a bundle with the value attached.
sort -ro{MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S16 | W
--why The option after the operand: getopt permutes, so --o=FILE still counts.
sort x.txt --o={MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-S17 | W
--why Other options before the abbreviated one.
sort -n -k 1,1 --ou {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S18 | W
--why --o=FILE with a here-document as the input.
sort --o={MEMORY}/a <<'EOF'
b
a
EOF

=== CRW-941-S19 | W
--why --ou FILE with a here-document as the input.
sort --ou {MEMORY}/a <<'EOF'
b
a
EOF

=== CRW-941-S20 | W
--why The value of --key is consumed, then --o FILE writes.
sort --key=1 --o {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S21 | W
--why -t, then the abbreviation.
sort -t, --o={MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S22 | W
--why A quoted value.
sort --o="{MEMORY}/a" x.txt

=== CRW-941-S23 | W
--why A pipe feeds the input.
cat x.txt | sort --o {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-S24 | W
--why The separate value of a long option that takes one (--compress-program) is consumed before --o.
sort --compress-program gzip --o {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S25 | W
--why The destination is an expansion the reader cannot evaluate: unknown, so the gate asks.
sort --o="$OUT" x.txt

=== CRW-941-S26 | W
--why sort -o in a bundle with a key option before it: -k takes its own value.
sort -k1,1 -o {MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S27 | W
--why A bundle of flags then --ou: -nr is no output.
sort -nr --ou={MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S28 | B
--why --o=FILE in the working directory writes outside the protected root.
sort --o=out.txt x.txt

=== CRW-941-S29 | B
--why --ou FILE in the working directory.
sort --ou out.txt x.txt

=== CRW-941-S30 | B
--why --o=FILE under the trusted temporary root.
sort --o={TMP}/out x.txt

=== CRW-941-S31 | B
--why After -- the word is an input file, not an option.
sort -- --o={MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-S32 | B
--why --s is ambiguous (--sort, --stable): sort refuses to run, nothing is written.
sort --s={MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S33 | B
--why --so=VALUE is --sort=VALUE, not an output.
sort --so={MEMORY}/a x.txt

=== CRW-941-S34 | B
--why The value of --key is read as the value: -o here is the key, and the memory file is an input.
sort --key -o {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-S35 | B
--why sort options that write nothing.
sort --reverse --unique --version-sort x.txt

=== CRW-941-S36 | B
--why Several short options, no output.
sort -u -n -k2,2 x.txt

=== CRW-941-E01 | W
--why --expression SCRIPT with the script as a separate argument.

=== CRW-941-E02 | W
--why --expression=SCRIPT.
sed --expression='w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E03 | W
--why --expr=SCRIPT, a prefix of --expression.
sed --expr='w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E04 | W
--why --expr SCRIPT with a separate argument.
sed --expr 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E05 | W
--why --exp SCRIPT.
sed --exp 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E06 | W
--why --e=SCRIPT: only --expression starts with e.
sed --e='w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E07 | W
--why --e SCRIPT.
sed --e 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E08 | W
--why --expressio=SCRIPT, one letter short.
sed --expressio='w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E09 | W
--why -n then --expression SCRIPT.
sed -n --expression 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E10 | W
--why Two --expression arguments; the second writes.
sed --expression p --expression 'W {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E11 | W
--why --expression SCRIPT with a here-document as the input.
sed --expression 'w {MEMORY}/a' <<'EOF'
abc
EOF

=== CRW-941-E12 | W
--why --exp=SCRIPT with a here-document as the input.
sed --exp='w {MEMORY}/a' <<'EOF'
abc
EOF

=== CRW-941-E13 | W
--why -eSCRIPT attached.
sed -e'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E14 | W
--why -ne SCRIPT in a bundle.
sed -ne 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E15 | W
--why The s///w flag in a later -e.
sed -n -e p -e 's/a/b/w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E16 | W
--why The script after -- is the first operand.
sed -n -- 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E17 | W
--why w after ; in the script.
sed 'p;w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E18 | W
--why w on the second line of the script.
sed 'p
w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E19 | W
--why The w flag after g.
sed 's/a/b/gw {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E20 | W
--why The w flag after a number.
sed 's/a/b/2w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E21 | W
--why s with another delimiter.
sed 'sxaxbxw {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E22 | W
--why w inside a block; the name runs to the end of the line.
sed -n '/x/{p;w {MEMORY}/a
}' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E23 | W
--why -E with a w flag.
sed -E 's/(a)/\1/w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E24 | W
--why -l takes a value; the script after it.
sed -l 5 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E25 | W
--why --line-length N then the script.
sed --line-length 5 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E26 | W
--why --line-length=N then the script.
sed --line-length=5 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E27 | W
--why --line N (a prefix) then the script.
sed --line 5 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E28 | W
--why -s with two inputs.
sed -s 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt y.txt

=== CRW-941-E29 | W
--why --quiet then the script.
sed --quiet 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E30 | W
--why --silent then the script.
sed --silent 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E31 | W
--why --regexp-extended then the script.
sed --regexp-extended 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E32 | W
--why --regexp (a prefix) then the script.
sed --regexp 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E33 | W
--why --null-data then the script.
sed --null-data 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E34 | W
--why --zero-terminated then the script.
sed --zero-terminated 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E35 | W
--why --z (a prefix of --zero-terminated) then the script.
sed --z 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E36 | W
--why --posix then the script.
sed --posix 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E37 | W
--why -z -u then the script.
sed -z -u 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E38 | W
--why GNU opens every w file when it compiles the script, so a w after q still creates and truncates the file.
sed 'q;w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E39 | W
--why q with an exit code, then w.
sed 'q5;w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E40 | W
--why l with a width, then w.
sed -n 'l 5;w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E41 | W
--why A branch whose label ends at the semicolon, then w.
sed 'b end;w {MEMORY}/a;:end' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E42 | W
--why A label ends at the semicolon, then w.
sed ':a;w {MEMORY}/a;ba' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E43 | W
--why w in a script given with -e and the input as a here-document.
sed -n -e p -e 'w {MEMORY}/a' <<'EOF'
abc
EOF

=== CRW-941-E44 | U
--why The file name is an expansion the reader cannot evaluate: the destination is unknown, so the gate asks.
sed "w $X/a" x.txt

=== CRW-941-E45 | W
--why T and t labels then w.
sed 't end;w {MEMORY}/a;:end' x.txt

=== CRW-941-E46 | W
--why Two inputs and an option after the script.
sed 'w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt -n

=== CRW-941-F01 | U

p
--cmd
sed --file s.sed x.txt

--file s.sed
p
--cmd

p
--cmd

p
--cmd

--file s.sed
p
--cmd

--why -fFILE attached.
--file s.sed
p
--cmd
sed -fs.sed x.txt

=== CRW-941-F07 | U
--why A script file next to an -e script.
--file s.sed
p
--cmd
sed -e p -f s.sed x.txt

=== CRW-941-F08 | U
--why --file=- reads the script from the here-document.
sed --file=- <<'EOF'
w {MEMORY}/a
EOF

=== CRW-941-F09 | U
--why --file - reads the script from the here-document.
sed --file - x.txt <<'EOF'
w {MEMORY}/a
EOF

=== CRW-941-F10 | U
--why The script file is written by the same text and then run.
printf 'w {MEMORY}/a\n' > s.sed; sed -f s.sed x.txt

=== CRW-941-F11 | U
--why The script file is a here-document written first and then run.
cat > s.sed <<'EOF'
w {MEMORY}/a
EOF
sed -f s.sed x.txt

=== CRW-941-F12 | U
--why --f is ambiguous (--file, --follow-symlinks): the reader refuses what it cannot prove.
--file s.sed
p
--cmd
sed --f s.sed x.txt

=== CRW-941-F13 | U
--why --s is ambiguous (--silent, --separate, --sandbox): refused.
sed --s p x.txt

=== CRW-941-F14 | U
--why An option outside the model.
sed --no-such-option p x.txt

=== CRW-941-I01 | W
--why -i rewrites its operand.
sed -i 's/a/b/' {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-I02 | W
--why --in-place rewrites its operand.
sed --in-place 's/a/b/' {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-I03 | W
--why --in (a prefix of --in-place) rewrites its operand.
sed --in 's/a/b/' {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-I04 | W
--why --i=SUFFIX rewrites its operand.
sed --i=.bak 's/a/b/' {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-I05 | W
--why --in-place=SUFFIX with -e.
sed --in-place=.bak -e p {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-I06 | W
--why -i with -e.
sed -i -e 's/a/b/' {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-I07 | W
--why -ni rewrites its operand.
sed -ni p {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-I08 | W
--why -i.bak rewrites its operand.
sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-I09 | W
--why --in-pl (a prefix) with --expression.
sed --in-pl --expression 's/a/b/' {MEMORY}/a

=== CRW-941-I10 | B
--why --in-place on a file in the working directory.
sed --in-place 's/a/b/' out.txt

=== CRW-941-I11 | B
--why --in=SUFFIX on a file in the working directory.
sed --in=.bak 's/a/b/' out.txt

=== CRW-941-C01 | B
--why --expression with a substitution writes nothing.
sed --expression 's/a/b/' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C02 | B
--why --expr=p writes nothing.
sed --expr=p x.txt

=== CRW-941-C03 | B
--why --quiet --expression=p writes nothing.
sed --quiet --expression=p x.txt

=== CRW-941-C04 | B
--why w in a pattern is no command.
sed -n -e 's/w/x/' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C05 | B
--why y with w characters.
sed 'y/w/x/' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C06 | B
--why A w in an address pattern is no command.
sed -n '/w a/p' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C07 | B
--why w to a file in the working directory.
sed 'w out.txt' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C08 | B
--why The w flag to a file in the working directory.
sed 's/a/b/w out.txt' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C09 | B
--why --expr with a w to a file in the working directory.
sed --expr='w out.txt' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C10 | B
--why w to /dev/stdout.
sed -e 'w /dev/stdout' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C11 | B
--why w to /dev/stderr.
sed --expression 'w /dev/stderr' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C12 | B
--why r reads the file, it does not write it.
sed 'r {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C13 | B
--why R reads the file.
sed 'R {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C14 | B
--why The text of a is no command.
sed 'a w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C15 | B
--why The text of i is no command.
sed '1i w {MEMORY}/a' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C16 | B
--why sed -n p with a here-document as the input.
sed -n p <<'EOF'
abc
EOF

=== CRW-941-C17 | B
--why The common join loop: a label, N, a branch.
sed ':a;N;$!ba;s/\n/ /g' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C18 | B
--why A block with p and q.
sed -n '/a/{p;q}' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C19 | B
--why A branch, a test and a label.
sed 's/a/b/;t end;s/c/d/;:end' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C20 | B
--why Delete lines.
sed '1d;$d' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C21 | B
--why -s -n with two inputs.
sed -s -n '$p' x.txt y.txt

=== CRW-941-C22 | B
--why -E with a group.
sed -E 's/(a|b)/\1/' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C23 | B
--why l with a width and q with a code.
sed -n 'l 5;q5' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C24 | B
--why sed in a pipe into sort -o in the working directory.
sed -n p x.txt | sort --o=out.txt

=== CRW-941-C25 | B
--why -e script, another -e script, no write.
sed -e 's/a/b/' -e 's/c/d/' x.txt

=== CRW-941-C26 | B
--why The script after -- is the first operand and writes nothing.
sed -n -- p x.txt

# After the pre-merge evaluation of 101be077 (d1 to d4): an unevaluated sort option value, POSIXLY_CORRECT option scanning,
# the backup suffix of sed -i, and sed script files that exist.

=== CRW-941-N01 | W
--why The value of -k is a word that splits into -k 1 -o FILE: the output option is hidden in an unknown word.
K='1 -o {MEMORY}/a'; sort -k $K x.txt

=== CRW-941-N02 | W
--why The same for the long option --key.
K='1 -o {MEMORY}/a'; sort --key $K x.txt

=== CRW-941-N03 | W
--why -S takes the unknown word as its value.
K='1G -o {MEMORY}/a'; sort -S $K x.txt

=== CRW-941-N04 | W
--why Another unknown value after a short bundle (-rt).
K=', -o {MEMORY}/a'; sort -rt $K x.txt

=== CRW-941-N05 | W
--why The value of --buffer-size= is attached to the option word: the whole word is unknown.
K='1G -o {MEMORY}/a'; sort --buffer-size=$K x.txt

=== CRW-941-N06 | B
--why A known value of -k is skipped, and -o names a file of the work tree.
K=1; sort -k $K -o out.txt x.txt

=== CRW-941-N07 | B
--why -k with a literal value and no output.
sort -k 2,2 -n x.txt

=== CRW-941-P01 | W
--why POSIXLY_CORRECT stops option scanning at the script: the first operand runs, and --e p is a file.
POSIXLY_CORRECT=1 sed 'w {MEMORY}/a' --e p x.txt

=== CRW-941-P02 | W
--why The same with --expression and a separate script word.
POSIXLY_CORRECT=1 sed 'w {MEMORY}/a' --expression p x.txt

=== CRW-941-P03 | W
--why The same with -e.
POSIXLY_CORRECT=1 sed 'w {MEMORY}/a' -e p x.txt

=== CRW-941-P04 | W
--why The same with -e in a bundle (-ne).
POSIXLY_CORRECT=1 sed 'w {MEMORY}/a' -ne p x.txt

=== CRW-941-P05 | W
--why The environment is exported before sed runs.
export POSIXLY_CORRECT=1; sed 'w {MEMORY}/a' --e p x.txt

=== CRW-941-P06 | W
--why Without the variable in the text the first operand may still be the script (the session environment): both readings are judged.
sed 'w {MEMORY}/a' --e p x.txt

=== CRW-941-P07 | W
--why The permuted reading (-e p is the script) writes nothing; the first operand is judged as well.
sed 'w {MEMORY}/a' -e p x.txt

=== CRW-941-P08 | Q
--why The first operand runs a shell command through the e command: POSIXLY_CORRECT hides it behind --expression.
POSIXLY_CORRECT=1 sed 'e gh pr comment 1 -b x' --expression p x.txt

=== CRW-941-P09 | B
--why No script option follows an operand: one reading.
sed -n p x.txt -n

=== CRW-941-P10 | B
--why The script option comes first; the operand after it is a file in both readings.
POSIXLY_CORRECT=1 sed -e p x.txt

=== CRW-941-P11 | B
--why Two scripts that write nothing, the second after the operand.
sed p -e p x.txt

=== CRW-941-D01 | W
--why The backup suffix of an abbreviation of --in-place moves the original into the memory root.
sed --in='{MEMORY}/*' -e p out.txt

=== CRW-941-D02 | W
--why -i with a suffix naming the memory root.
sed -i'{MEMORY}/*' p out.txt

=== CRW-941-D03 | W
--why -ni with a suffix, the original in a subdirectory of the work tree.
sed -ni'{MEMORY}/*.bak' p sub/out.txt

=== CRW-941-D04 | W
--why --in-place= with the full option name.
sed --in-place='{MEMORY}/*' p out.txt

=== CRW-941-D05 | W
--why A relative suffix that reaches the memory root by ..; the working directory is below it.
sed -i'{MEMORY}/../memories/*' p out.txt

=== CRW-941-D06 | B
--why A suffix without * is appended to the name (out.txt/...): the backup stays under the input, never in the memory root.
sed -i'{MEMORY}/x' p out.txt

=== CRW-941-D07 | B
--why A backup suffix without * or a slash stays next to the input.
sed -i.bak p out.txt

=== CRW-941-D08 | B
--why A backup directory of the work tree.
sed -i'bak/*' p out.txt

=== CRW-941-D09 | B
--why A * suffix that keeps the name.
sed -i'*.orig' p out.txt

=== CRW-941-D10 | B
--why A later -i without a suffix replaces the earlier suffix: no backup.
sed -i'{MEMORY}/*' -i p out.txt

=== CRW-941-F15 | U
--why The script file exists and holds a command that runs a shell command (e).
--file s.sed
e rm -rf {CHECKOUT}
--cmd
sed -f s.sed x.txt

=== CRW-941-F16 | U
--why The script file exists and holds a w command to the memory root.
--file s.sed
w {MEMORY}/a
--cmd
sed --file=s.sed x.txt

=== CRW-941-D11 | W
--why POSIXLY_CORRECT stops getopt at out.txt: the later --in-place is a file name and the suffix of the earlier --in stays the backup place (evaluation of the d3 fix, 83a490cef).
POSIXLY_CORRECT=1 sed --in='{MEMORY}/*' -e p out.txt --in-place

=== CRW-941-D12 | W
--why The same with a later -i: it does not replace the suffix in the POSIXLY_CORRECT reading.
sed --in='{MEMORY}/*' -e p out.txt -i

=== CRW-941-D13 | W
--why The same with a later -i.bak.
sed --in='{MEMORY}/*' -e p out.txt -i.bak

=== CRW-941-D14 | W
--why The same with a later --in-place=.bak.
sed --in='{MEMORY}/*' -e p out.txt --in-place=.bak

=== CRW-941-D15 | W
--why The later option is a bundle -ni.
sed -i'{MEMORY}/*' p out.txt -ni

=== CRW-941-D16 | B
--why A later option after an earlier suffix without a place: the backup stays next to the input.
sed -i.bak -e p out.txt -i
